questions.question: Why does LLMOps need to monitor output quality, not just traditional metrics like uptime and latency?
options: Uptime and latency are not real concerns for AI applications
An LLM response can have a healthy status code and fast latency while still being unhelpful, off-topic, or subtly wrong — a dimension traditional monitoring doesn't capture
LLM applications never experience uptime or latency issues
Quality monitoring replaces the need for uptime monitoring entirely
questions.explanation: Traditional operational metrics can look perfectly healthy while output quality silently regresses, since a 'successful' response (200 status, fast) doesn't guarantee the content itself is actually good.

questions.question: Why can a prompt or model change affect production behavior without showing up in a traditional code deployment log?
options: Prompt and model changes are always tracked identically to code changes
Prompts can be edited independently of code deploys, and model providers can make updates on their end, both of which can change behavior without a traditional code deployment ever happening
This scenario is purely theoretical and never actually happens
Only code changes can ever affect an LLM application's behavior
questions.explanation: Unlike traditional software where behavior changes are tied to code deploys, LLM application behavior can shift due to prompt edits or provider-side model updates, which traditional deployment tracking may not capture.

questions.question: Users complain an AI feature's quality has declined, but all traditional dashboards (uptime, latency, error rate) look healthy. Which question best identifies the gap?
options: Should we conclude the users are simply mistaken?
Do we have any continuous signal for output quality, and would we have noticed this regression before users started complaining?
Should we just restart the servers to fix this?
Is this definitely a rate-limiting issue?
questions.explanation: This is a textbook case of a quality regression invisible to traditional monitoring — the fix is establishing continuous quality monitoring as a first-class operational signal, not just relying on traditional uptime/latency dashboards.
